# @agentex/agent

Programmatic execution of AI coding agents. Spawn and manage Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, Gemini, Cursor, OpenCode, Pi, OpenClaw, or any CLI-based agent as a child process with streaming output, multi-turn sessions, auth detection, isolated workspaces, skill installation, and a unified interface.

## Install

```bash
npm install @agentex/agent
```

Node.js >= 20.19. Each provider requires its CLI to be installed and on `$PATH`. The Codex session adapter additionally requires **codex-cli 0.130.0 or newer** (the `app-server` subcommand); older CLIs will fail with `unexpected argument '--json'`.

## Quick Start

```typescript
import { getProvider } from "@agentex/agent";

const claude = getProvider("claude");

const result = await claude.execute({
  prompt: "Add error handling to server.ts",
  config: {
    skipPermissions: true,
    maxTurns: 5,
    timeoutSec: 120,
  },
  onEvent: (event) => {
    if (event.type === "assistant") process.stdout.write(event.text);
    if (event.type === "tool_call") console.log(`Tool ${event.name} (toolCallId=${event.toolCallId})`);
    // event.sessionId, event.messageId, event.eventId are populated per-provider
  },
});

console.log(result.status);     // "completed"
console.log(result.summary);    // "Added try/catch to all route handlers..."
console.log(result.durationMs); // 12340
console.log(result.costUsd);    // 0.0342
console.log(result.usage);      // { "claude-sonnet-4-6": { inputTokens: 1200, outputTokens: 350, costUsd: 0.0342, ... } }
console.log(result.stopReason); // "end_turn"
console.log(result.numTurns);   // 3
console.log(result.rateLimits); // [{ status: "allowed", ... }]
console.log(result.raw);        // the final provider-native event, verbatim (escape hatch)
```

## Built-in Providers

Providers fall into three tiers:

- **Tier 1 — deep native:** `claude`, `codex`. Hand-built adapters over each CLI's richest protocol (Claude's stream-json, Codex's `app-server` JSON-RPC). Subscription-native, fullest feature set.
- **Tier 2 — ACP:** `gemini`, `copilot`, plus any agent registered via [`acpProvider`](#custom--byok-providers) or `extends: "acp"` config. One shared, tested base over the open [Agent Client Protocol](https://agentclientprotocol.com) (JSON-RPC over stdio).
- **Tier 3 — bespoke escape hatches:** `opencode` (authenticated HTTP/SSE daemon), `pi` (persistent RPC), `antigravity` (persistent stream-json), `cursor` (exec-backed resume), `openclaw` (HTTP gateway), `process` (any executable).

| Provider   | Transport                              | Tier | Sessions  | Modes | Permissions |
| ---------- | -------------------------------------- | ---- | --------- | ----- | ----------- |
| `claude`   | `claude` CLI stream-json               | 1    | ✅ resume | —     | ✅          |
| `codex`    | `codex app-server` JSON-RPC            | 1    | ✅ resume | ✅    | ✅          |
| `gemini`   | `gemini --acp` (ACP)                   | 2    | ✅        | ✅    | ✅          |
| `copilot`  | `copilot --acp` (ACP)                  | 2    | ✅        | ✅    | ✅          |
| `opencode` | authenticated `opencode serve` HTTP + SSE | 3 | ✅ resume | ✅ | ✅ |
| `pi`       | persistent `pi --mode rpc`             | 3    | ✅ resume | —     | —           |
| `antigravity` | persistent `agy` stream-json (stdin + stdout) | 3 | ✅ resume | ✅ | policy |
| `cursor`   | `cursor-agent` stream-json per turn    | 3    | ✅ resume | probed | —          |
| `openclaw` | HTTP gateway                           | 3    | —         | —     | —           |
| `process`  | any executable                         | 3    | —         | —     | —           |

Cursor sessions are exec-backed. Each `send()` starts one CLI process and promotes the returned Cursor session ID into `--resume` for the next turn. `probeCapabilities()` verifies the selected binary's model catalog and advertised modes. Each execution independently validates the supported stream-json acceptance marker before releasing output. Older Cursor CLIs report `upgrade_required` instead of silently advertising discovery features they do not expose.

### Codex sessions: approvals and the sandbox

A Codex session is one `codex app-server` process. That subcommand drops the interactive `--sandbox` and `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` flags, so agentex sets the approval policy and sandbox through root `-c` overrides and again on `thread/start` / `thread/resume`:

| Config | Approval policy | Sandbox |
| ------ | --------------- | ------- |
| `skipPermissions` | `never` | `danger-full-access` |
| `planMode` (wins over `skipPermissions`) | Codex's default | `read-only` |
| neither | Codex's default (`on-request`) | Codex's default (depends on the folder's trust) |

Under `never` with full access, Codex approves MCP and ChatGPT app tool calls itself. With approvals on, it asks first, and agentex passes the question to `onUserInputRequest` as a tool permission:

- `toolName` is `mcp__<server>__<tool>`, the name the model calls (`mcp__codex_apps__github_create_branch` for the GitHub app).
- `toolUseId` is the call's item id, the same `toolCallId` its `tool_call` event carries. When the call can't be matched, it is a fresh `codex-mcp-approval-<uuid>`.
- `title` is Codex's question (`Allow GitHub to run tool "create_branch"?`), `description` the parameters it shows (`Repository: acme/web · Branch name: fix/login`), and `input` the call's arguments.
- `{ allow: true }` runs that one call. `{ allow: false }` declines it, and the call fails with "user rejected MCP tool call".

An MCP server's own form or URL request goes to `onElicitation`, and is declined without one. MCP and app calls surface as `tool_call` / `tool_result` events under the same `mcp__<server>__<tool>` name.

Codex CLI 0.160+ also honors `config.mcpServers` for both `execute()` and new/resumed sessions. Attached configurations default to strict isolation from ambient configured MCP servers; set `strictMcpConfig: false` to retain them. Header values and stdio environment values stay out of argv, and `CODEX_HOME`, auth and history remain in place. Host-supplied servers enforce their own tool policy and are automatically approved by Codex, avoiding duplicate host permission requests. Other servers and native ChatGPT apps retain the approval behavior above. See the [Codex MCP guide](docs/codex-mcp.md) for configuration, runtime requirements and verified resume behavior.

### Antigravity (Google)

Google moved personal accounts (Free, Google AI Pro, Google AI Ultra) from Gemini CLI to the [Antigravity CLI](https://antigravity.google/docs/cli/overview) on 2026-06-18. Signing in to Gemini CLI with one of those accounts now fails with "This client is no longer supported for Gemini Code Assist for individuals". Use the `antigravity` provider for them. The `gemini` provider still works with a paid API key or Gemini Code Assist Standard/Enterprise.

```bash
curl -fsSL https://antigravity.google/cli/install.sh | bash   # installs ~/.local/bin/agy
agy                                                            # once, to sign in through the browser
```

```typescript
const agy = getProvider("antigravity");
const session = await agy.createSession!({
  cwd,
  config: { model: "gemini-3.1-pro-high", effort: "high", modeId: "accept-edits" },
  onEvent: (e) => { if (e.type === "assistant") console.log(e.text); },
});
await (await session.send("Summarize this repo")).result;
await (await session.send("Now list its entry points")).result; // same agy process, same conversation
```

- **Transport.** A session is one `agy --input-format stream-json --output-format stream-json` process. Each `send()` writes one NDJSON user message and resolves on that turn's `result` event. `execute()` writes one message and closes stdin, so prompts never travel through argv. Saved `sessionParams` are `{ sessionId, cwd }` and resume with `--conversation`. Antigravity scopes conversations to a directory, so params saved for another `cwd` start a new conversation instead of resuming.
- **Interrupts.** The CLI has no control protocol, so `interrupt()`, timeouts, and abort signals send SIGINT to the process group, like Ctrl+C. If agy exits instead of reporting the turn as `INTERRUPTED`, the next `send()` starts a new process on the same conversation.
- **Permissions.** Headless agy cannot ask. `skipPermissions` maps to `--dangerously-skip-permissions`. Without it, actions that would need approval (shell commands by default) are soft-denied and listed in `ExecutionResult.permissionDenials`, and the run still succeeds. Grant specific actions with `permissions.allow` rules in `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/settings.json`. `permissionRequests` is therefore `false`.
- **Modes, effort, models.** `listModes()` returns `default`, `accept-edits`, and `plan`. agy's `--mode` accepts only `accept-edits` and `plan`, so `default` passes no flag and agy uses the `agentMode` saved in its settings.json (request-review unless changed). `planMode` maps to `--mode plan`. Plan mode, however it is requested, suppresses `--dangerously-skip-permissions`. `config.effort` maps to `--effort` (`low`, `medium`, `high`, `max`). `listModels()` reads `agy models`, which needs a signed-in account.
- **Instructions.** agy has no system-prompt flag, so `instructionsFile` rides on the first message each agy process accepts, like a per-process system prompt. Every `execute()` and every new session sends it, including resumes, so a saved conversation agy can no longer find still gets it. It stays pending until agy acknowledges a message that carried it, so a failed start or sign-in does not drop it. A session that respawns agy on a conversation it already briefed does not repeat it.
- **Skills.** `skillDirs` go in a temporary folder of links (`.agents/skills/<name>`) that every agy process a run or session starts gets with `--add-dir`, removed when the run ends or the session closes. Nothing global changes, so a chat's skills never reach other agy sessions. Headless agy refuses to read a file whose real path is outside its workspace, linked or not, so unless it skips permissions each skill's own folder is added too (one already under `cwd` isn't), or the agent would see the skill and be denied its `SKILL.md`. Links keep a skill edited mid-chat current. agy 1.4.3 reads global skills from `~/.gemini/config/skills` and project skills from `.agents/skills`, never `~/.agents/skills`, and gives the agent nothing from `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/skills`, where agentex 0.0.40–0.0.45 linked `skillDirs`. A run or session removes the links those versions left there for its skills, and any link there that leads nowhere.
- **Sign-in.** An unsigned headless agy prints a login URL and waits a minute for a code. agentex stops it as soon as the prompt appears, emits `auth_required` with `loginCommand: "agy"`, and fails the turn with `errorCode: "auth_required"`.
- **Usage.** agy reports cumulative usage per process. agentex reports each turn's share, keyed by the pinned model (or `"default"`). `cachedInputTokens` comes from `cache_read_tokens`.
- **Not yet wired.** `config.mcpServers` (agy reads `~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json` and `.agents/mcp_config.json` itself), and history import.

OpenCode sessions use a password-authenticated loopback server, SSE events, permission and question reconciliation, durable service-backed history, saved-session discovery and import, runtime model and agent discovery, and upstream provider authentication. `config.mcpServers` remains unsupported for OpenCode because strict isolation from ambient OpenCode MCP configuration is not yet proven.

### OpenCode and Cursor discovery

The static `capabilities` object describes the maximum adapter surface. Use the runtime probe before presenting controls that depend on a particular installed CLI version.

```ts
const opencode = getProvider("opencode");
const runtime = await opencode.probeCapabilities?.({ cwd });
const models = runtime?.capabilities.modelDiscovery?.supported
  ? await opencode.listModels?.({ cwd })
  : [];
const modes = runtime?.capabilities.modes?.supported
  ? await opencode.listModes?.({ cwd })
  : [];

const cursor = getProvider("cursor");
const cursorRuntime = await cursor.probeCapabilities?.({ cwd });
const cursorModels = cursorRuntime?.capabilities.modelDiscovery?.supported
  ? await cursor.listModels?.({ cwd })
  : [];
```

OpenCode model IDs are fully qualified as `provider/model`. Provider-native variants are returned separately on `ProviderModel.variants` and selected with `config.modelVariant`. Cursor models are returned exactly as the installed CLI reports them. Grok therefore appears through Cursor discovery when the account and CLI expose it. There is no separate Grok provider or hard-coded Grok catalog.

Cursor's runtime report claims sessions and resume only when the selected CLI advertises `--print`, `--resume`, and `stream-json` as an explicit `--output-format` value. A generic output-format flag is not enough. A real turn still validates that `system:init` arrives before releasing any output. This keeps discovery non-billable without treating a successful model-list command as proof of the execution protocol.

OpenCode also exposes its upstream providers so an app can build provider-first credential UI without storing keys in agentex:

```ts
const manager = opencode.upstreamProviders!;
const providers = await manager.list({ cwd });
const methods = await manager.authMethods("anthropic", { cwd });
await manager.setApiKey("anthropic", apiKey, { cwd });
```

OAuth uses `beginOAuth()` followed by `completeOAuth()`. Disconnect is capability-gated against the running OpenCode schema. The tested OpenCode 1.3.2 profile uses `DELETE /auth/{providerID}`. Unknown credential-ID schemas are reported unsupported instead of guessing which credential to delete.

Capabilities (sessions, modes, skills, workspaces, MCP, model discovery, quota probing, instructions, concurrent send, cancel queued messages, stop task) are declared on each module's `capabilities` field — check `provider.capabilities` to branch on what's supported. ACP providers set `dynamicCapabilities: true` (their real capability set is negotiated at the ACP `initialize` handshake). Skill-aware providers also report:

- `skillInventory` — `"provider-init"` for Claude's runtime inventory, `"local-discovery"` for Codex, or `"none"`.
- `skillInvocation` — `"native-slash"` for Claude, `"expanded-prompt"` for Codex, `"configured-only"`, or `"unsupported"`.

## Custom / BYOK providers

Three ways to add providers without forking, all behind the same `getProvider` /
`ProviderModule` surface. See [internal-docs/spec-provider-architecture.md](../../internal-docs/spec-provider-architecture.md)
for the design.

**Derived providers (config-extend).** Inherit a built-in with an env / command /
model overlay — the canonical use is pointing Claude at an Anthropic-compatible
gateway:

```ts
import { defineDerivedProvider, registerProvider, loadProvidersFromConfig } from "@agentex/agent";

registerProvider(
  defineDerivedProvider({
    id: "zai",
    extends: "claude",
    env: { ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL: "https://api.z.ai/api/anthropic", ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN: "…" },
    models: [{ id: "glm-5.1", name: "GLM 5.1" }],
  }),
);

// …or load a whole map from config (also accepts Paseo's `agents.providers` nesting):
loadProvidersFromConfig({
  providers: {
    zai: { extends: "claude", env: { ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL: "…" } },
    "my-gemini": { extends: "acp", command: ["gemini", "--acp"] },
  },
});
```

When the base provider supports durable sessions or service history, the
derived provider keeps that capability without losing its identity. Persisted
records use the derived provider ID, and attachment/resume reapplies the
derived command, environment, mode, cwd, and session parameters. Upstream
provider authentication and disconnect calls also receive the derived runtime
overlay, so an OpenCode provider configured with an isolated credential home
continues to use that store for credential management.

## API Reference

### Registry
- `getProvider(type)` — look up a registered provider. Throws if unknown.
- `listProviders()` — list all registered provider type names.
- `registerProvider(module)` — register a custom provider.

### Execution
- `provider.execute(ctx)` — run a single turn.
- `provider.createSession?(ctx)` — start a multi-turn session (when `capabilities.sessions`).
- `executeAll(tasks, { cancelOnFailure?, signal? })` — run multiple executions concurrently.

### Auth
- `provider.resolveAuth(ctx?)` — structured report: binary status, all auth paths, identity. Cached 60s; pass `{ fresh: true }` to bypass.
- `hasSubscription(provider, ctx?)` / `hasApiKey(provider, ctx?)` / `hasBedrock(provider, ctx?)` — presence sugar.
- `clearAuthCache()` — invalidate the resolveAuth cache globally (e.g. after a login).
- `detectAuth(providerType, env)` — legacy env-only auth classification used internally for `ExecutionResult.billingType`.

### Binary / runtime
- `findBinary(name, configOverride?)` — resolve a provider CLI on disk.
- `ensureCommandResolvable(command)` — like `findBinary` but accepts an absolute path too.
- `clearBinaryCache()` — invalidate the binary-resolution cache.
- `provider.checkQuota?(ctx)` — deprecated legacy quota surface. Claude returns unmeasured/unknown capacity; use `session.rateLimits`.
- `session.contextUsage?.getSnapshot(options?)` / `session.rateLimits?.getSnapshot(options?)` — independent, synchronous observations with no provider request.
- `session.contextUsage?.refresh?.()` / `session.rateLimits?.refresh?.()` — explicit bounded native reads, when supported by the selected runtime/auth context.
- `provider.listModels?(opts?)` — enumerate models the binary can drive, where the CLI exposes a catalog (for example `cursor`, `opencode`, and `antigravity` via `agy models`). Otherwise pass the model you want directly via `ExecutionContext.model` or `ProviderConfig.model`.

### Workspace
- `prepareWorkspace({ strategy, baseBranch?, branchName?, targetDir? })` → `PreparedWorkspace` with `cwd`, `diff()`, `cleanup()`.

### Skills
- `installSkills(skillDirs, opts?)` / `removeSkills(skillDirs, opts?)` / `listInstalledSkills(opts?)` — standard channels by `location`, plus native folders with `includeNativeDirs`, or exactly the `folders` named. `installSkills` takes `replaceDeadLinks`.
- `resolveSkillsHome(channel)` / `resolveSkillsWorkspace(channel, cwd)`
- `resolveNativeSkillsHome(runtime)` / `resolveNativeSkillsWorkspace(runtime, cwd)`
- `ensureSkillSymlink(...)`
- `commandInventoryFromEvent(event)` — extract provider-reported slash/skill names from a `system/init` event.
- `discoverSkillCommands({ cwd?, skillDirs?, includeInstalled?, runtime? })` — parse local `SKILL.md` metadata into `SkillCommandDescriptor[]`.
- `reconcileSkillCommands({ discovered, inventory?, provider, appCommands? })` — merge app commands and apply provider runtime availability.
- `formatSlashInvocation(command, args?)` — build `/name args` text.
- `invokeSkill(session, command, options?)` — send native slash text for `provider-slash` commands or an expanded prompt for `expanded-prompt` commands.
- `buildExpandedSkillPrompt(command, options?)` — construct the expanded-prompt payload without sending it.

### Runtime config
- `withTempConfig({ runtime, seedFromDefault?, overrides? })` → env + configDir + cleanup.
- `getRuntimeHomeEnvVar(runtime)` / `getDefaultRuntimeHome(runtime)` — introspect each CLI's home dir override.

### Utilities
- `aggregateUsage(usage)` — collapse `Record<string, TokenUsage>` to a single total.
- `renderTemplate(template, ctx)` — `{{var}}` interpolation.
- `redactEnvForLogs(env)` — redact sensitive values before logging.
- `resolveInstructions(path?)` — read an instructions file, or `null` if no path.
- `installInstructions(content, opts?)` / `removeInstructions(opts?)` — write/remove a managed instruction brief across per-runtime files (`AGENTS.md`, plus opt-in native `CLAUDE.md` pointer / `GEMINI.md`), workspace or global.
- `resolveInstructionTargets(opts?)` — list which instruction files would be written, without touching disk.
- `upsertManagedBlock(existing, content, opts?)` / `stripManagedBlock(existing, opts?)` — low-level managed-region merge/strip (preserves content outside the markers).
- `getDefaultRuntimeHome(runtime, homeDir?)` — pass `homeDir` to resolve against a sandboxed base instead of `os.homedir()`.
- `parseAskUserQuestion(req)` — extract structured question/option data from a `UserInputRequest`.
- `parseExitPlanMode(req)` — extract the proposed plan text from an `ExitPlanMode` permission request (Claude plan mode).

## Requirements

- Node.js >= 18
- Each provider's CLI installed and resolvable on `$PATH` (`claude`, `codex`, `agy` for Antigravity, `gemini`, `agent` for Cursor, `opencode`, `pi`, or a reachable OpenClaw gateway). `agy` is also found at `~/.local/bin/agy` when that folder is not on `$PATH`.
- For subscription auth, the relevant CLI must already be logged in (`codex login`, `claude login`, `agy` once for Antigravity, etc.)

## Session titles

Native title metadata and generation are separate capabilities. Claude exposes
`readTitle`, `setTitle` and `generateNativeTitle` in verified CLI versions. Codex
exposes `readTitle` and `setTitle` through app-server, and reports name changes as
`title_changed` events. Codex has no native generation RPC. Other providers omit
these optional controls until their native protocols are supported.

```ts
import { generateTitle } from "@agentex/agent";

const existing = await session.readTitle?.();
const suggestion = existing ? { title: existing, source: "native" as const } :
  await generateTitle(session, {
    description: userRequest,
    signal,
    fallbackTitleGenerator: ({ description, signal, reason, error }) =>
      myApp.generateTitle(description, { signal, reason, error }),
  });
// Recheck the host's title revision before saving or synchronizing a suggestion.
if (suggestion && myApp.canApplyTitle()) {
  myApp.saveTitle(suggestion);
  await session.setTitle?.(suggestion.title);
}
```

`generateTitle` is a shared helper, not a provider-generated turn. It invokes
actual native generation when available, and invokes the supplied fallback once
on unsupported, empty, or failed generation. Without a supplied fallback it
returns null. Cancellation propagates immediately and never starts a fallback.
Fallback failures propagate. Results report `source: "native" | "fallback"`.
Neither the helper nor native generation persists a suggestion. Reading an old
name is deliberately separate, so a fresh retrospective request stays fresh.
The library supplies no title prompt, model, automatic trigger, or fallback.

`ProviderCapabilities` declares maximum native `sessionTitleRead`,
`sessionTitleWrite`, and `nativeTitleGeneration` support. Runtime probes report
verified installed-version support (Claude 2.1.295 and Codex 0.160.0 minimums for
controls). Native requests are bounded and may fail on changed CLI protocols.
`title_changed` is metadata, not conversational content, and only reflects
changes the session observes. Claude reads bounded transcript metadata without
rewriting it. All title writes go through the CLI's native control protocol.

## Unreleased

- Add first-class `ProviderConfig.serviceTier` for Codex Standard/Fast/Ultrafast and Claude Code Standard/Fast across execution, new sessions, and resume. Omission inherits native behavior; `default` explicitly selects Standard. Speed stays independent of model and effort, and unsupported or conflicting explicit choices fail before inference with `ServiceTierConfigurationError`.
- Codex sends explicit tiers through app-server start/resume/turn, including one-shot execution, so a saved thread's speed cannot silently override the requested tier. Validate feature gates and the actual selected model's native catalog. Claude merges `fastMode` into private temporary settings, requires an explicit supported Opus model for Fast, and cleans up on completion, close, or process exit.
- Expose model tier metadata, installed-runtime capabilities, and requested/selected/effective observations on events, sessions, turns, and execution results. Native fallback notifications remain visible; requested speed never implies billed speed. Discovery honors endpoints, profiles, and effective environment with credential-hashed cache identities.
- Gateway agent configs forward `serviceTier`. Add regression coverage and an installed-CLI smoke script using a local fake API, including Codex tier changes on the same resumed thread. See [inference speed](docs/inference-speed.md).
- Preserve Codex cross-directory/worktree isolation for typed-tier execution, verify the native working directory, and cover startup RPCs with cancellation and deadlines. Retain per-turn input, output, and cached-token accounting from native notifications, with fallback scans using the child's Codex home.
- Reject Claude Fast on known unsupported cloud routes using effective endpoint/settings routing, and resolve `opus[1m]` before checking model support. Discovery cache identities now fingerprint native credential files without reading their contents, sharing telemetry's file-identity helper.

## 0.0.48 — Codex chats stop writing skills into the project

- **Codex `skillDirs` no longer go in the project.** Codex runs and sessions linked a chat's `skillDirs` into `{cwd}/.agents/skills` and never removed them, so they turned up in the project's git status, got committed (Ri's repo carries five), reached every later Codex session in that folder and every worktree made from it, and two chats sharing a folder saw each other's skills. Now each session stages its skills in a temporary folder of links and hands it to `codex app-server` with `skills/extraRoots/set` before its thread starts or resumes, and removes it when the session closes or its process exits. Verified live against codex-cli 0.163.0: a root's linked and real skill folders are used, nothing is written to the project or `~/.codex/config.toml`, another app-server in the same folder sees none of them, and two concurrent sessions in one git repo each used only their own skills while `git status` stayed empty.
- **One-shot runs with skills go through `codex app-server`.** `codex exec` can't take skills except from folders every Codex session scans (neither `--add-dir` nor a `skills.config` path entry gives a run a skill), so a run with `skillDirs` now runs one turn on the session's app-server. It keeps what `codex exec` does: approvals `never` (a session with no host handler would otherwise accept every escalation), the same sandbox, live web search for `search` (`-c web_search="live"`), and one `timeoutSec` and `signal` over the whole run: a stalled startup times out or cancels like a stalled turn, with the process stopped and the skills removed. `exec` flags in `extraArgs` are translated to app-server fields (`-m`, `-s`, the bypass flag, `-i`, `--output-schema`, `-o`, `--ephemeral`), the output-only ones are dropped, and any other fails the run with `errorCode: "unsupported_args"` before it starts, instead of crashing app-server on an unknown argument. Instructions go in as developer instructions instead of ahead of the prompt, the run reports the app-server's pid, and a startup failure rejects after removing any workspace, as a session's does. Runs without skills still use `codex exec`. Verified live, including resuming the run's thread, a schema-shaped answer from `--output-schema`, and an `--ephemeral` thread Codex kept no record of.

```typescript

    ],
    strictMcpConfig: true,
  },
  onElicitation: async (request) => showMcpForm(request),

Use the actual signed credential header name expected by your server. HTTP transport means streamable HTTP. Codex does not support the legacy `sse` arm of `McpServerConfig`; that configuration is rejected.

## Isolation and configuration

- Supplying `mcpServers` defaults Codex to strict isolation, including an explicitly empty array.
- `strictMcpConfig: true` without servers disables all ambient configured MCP servers.
- `strictMcpConfig: false` retains the user's configured servers alongside the attached servers.
- Omitting both options preserves the existing ambient Codex behavior.
- Host names must be unique and nonempty. `codex_apps` is reserved. A name that already exists in ambient configuration is rejected, even if disabled, because native config merging could otherwise inherit its transport, credentials or per-tool policy. Choose a distinct host name.

Codex merges user, project, profile and managed config layers. An empty `mcp_servers` table does not remove inherited servers. Agent Ex reads the effective inventory through bounded `codex mcp list --json` calls, emits disabled registrations for ambient servers, then verifies the final enabled set before starting the session. This includes plugin-derived configured servers: a disabled config registration vetoes the same-name plugin registration in the verified runtime. Disabled servers can remain visible in Codex's status inventory; they have no initialized connection or model-visible tools.

Config overrides are placed before `app-server` or `exec`, including on resume. Caller config flags from `extraArgs` are included in discovery and precede the final MCP security overrides. If inventory discovery fails, a requested host server is blocked by policy, or an unrelated server remains enabled under strict isolation, startup fails with a credential-safe error. Native inventory stdout/stderr is not forwarded to user callbacks.

MCP-configured resumes explicitly select the working directory used for inventory discovery. Supply the original project as `cwd`, or retain the `cwd` in restored `sessionParams` when omitting the context's `cwd`. This prevents an old thread from loading unverified servers from another project. Use the context's `cwd` and `ProviderConfig.workspace` for project selection; `--cd`/`-C` and `--worktree` in `extraArgs` are rejected when MCP configuration is requested because native inventory does not apply those runtime options.

`CODEX_HOME` is never replaced. No user config file is rewritten, so subscription auth, history and existing native settings continue to use the original home. Every invocation gets its own environment-variable names; concurrent sessions cannot overwrite one another's MCP credentials.

This option isolates **configured MCP servers**. Codex's native ChatGPT apps integration is separate and retains its existing configuration and approval behavior. This release does not change that integration's enablement or connected-account scope.

## Credentials and stdio environment

HTTP bearer auth uses `bearer_token_env_var`. Other headers use `env_http_headers`. Only variable references enter native `-c` overrides; the values exist in the spawned Codex environment. Embedded URL user/password credentials are rejected; put authentication in headers.

Stdio servers without environment overrides retain their command and arguments directly. When a server has `env`, a small Node transport launcher receives the command, arguments and environment through a unique child-only variable, overlays that server's environment, removes Agent Ex's credential variables before launching the server, and forwards shutdown signals. This preserves different values for two servers using the same environment key without exposing those values in argv or changing the host process environment. No temporary credential file is created.

Commands, plain stdio arguments and public URLs are configuration visible in argv. Supply credentials through `headers` or stdio `env`.

## Permissions and names

Host-supplied servers receive `default_tools_approval_mode = "approve"`. If Codex still emits a tool-approval request for one of them, Agent Ex accepts it without calling `onUserInputRequest`. The host server must enforce its own tool policy, including any ask-first/write confirmation. Other server and ChatGPT app approvals still reach the host normally. Form/URL elicitations from all servers, including host-owned ones, still go to `onElicitation` and are declined when no handler exists.

Normalized tool events and approval names retain `mcp__<server>__<tool>` with the existing Codex name sanitizer. The actual model-visible namespace can also depend on native Codex configuration; consuming apps should use the normalized events for correlation rather than inventing another naming scheme.

# Concurrent Send for AgentSession

## Context

`AgentSession.send()` currently throws if a turn is already in progress:

```ts
// providers/claude/session.ts:271, providers/codex/session.ts:286
if (this._state !== "idle") throw new Error("A turn is already in progress");
```

But both Claude Code and Codex CLIs natively support receiving user messages mid-turn — the CLI internally queues them and either (a) drains them as `<system-reminder>` attachments on the next tool result batch, or (b) starts a new turn coalescing queued items when the current turn ends. Our guard prevents apps from using this UX.

This spec relaxes the guard, exposes a capability flag, and adds queue-cancellation where the upstream CLI supports it — bringing Agentex to feature parity with Claude Code's own TUI for the "type while it's working" workflow.

## Goals

1. Concurrent `send()` is the default API contract — no opt-in. For Claude and Codex (the flagship providers), the call passes straight through to the CLI's native queue.
2. Apps can cancel a queued (not-yet-processed) message by UUID, for providers whose CLI supports it.
3. Library generates UUIDs; apps don't have to manage them. Returned from `send()` for use with `cancel()`.
4. Public API surface stays small: existing `send / interrupt / close` plus one new `cancel(uuid)` method.
5. Apps can read `provider.capabilities` to gate UX, but don't have to know about it to use the API correctly.

## Non-goals

- No `peek` / `list queued` API. App tracks its own unacked sends (it has the UUIDs from `send()`).
- No retraction of messages that have already started processing (mid-turn drain has already injected them; nothing to remove).
- No in-adapter buffering for providers without native concurrent-send. Such providers throw on concurrent `send()`. App can layer its own queue if needed.
- No changes to `interrupt()` semantics (abort the in-flight turn) or `close()`.

## Design

### Public API

```ts
interface SendHandle {
  /** UUID generated by the library, attached to the user message. Use with cancel(). */
  uuid: string;
  /** Resolves with the next TurnResult after the message was written. May be shared with other concurrent sends. */
  result: Promise<TurnResult>;
}

interface AgentSession {
  readonly sessionId: string | null;
  readonly state: SessionState;

  /**
   * Send a user message. Returns the message's UUID synchronously plus a
   * promise for the resulting TurnResult.
   *
   * Callable at any time (including while a turn is in progress) for providers
   * whose CLI supports it natively — the CLI's own queue handles ordering.
   * For providers that don't support concurrent send, calling while !idle
   * throws. Check `provider.capabilities.concurrentSend` to gate UX if needed.
   *
   * If multiple sends are coalesced or drained into one turn by the CLI, their
   * `result` Promises resolve with the same TurnResult object.
   */
  send(message: string): Promise<SendHandle>;

  /**
   * Cancel a previously-sent message that is still queued in the CLI.
   *
   * Always callable. Returns {cancelled: false} when:
   *   - The provider doesn't support per-message cancellation (capabilities.cancelQueuedMessage === false)
   *   - The message has already been dequeued (race lost to mid-turn drain)
   *   - The UUID is unknown to the CLI
   */
  cancel(uuid: string): Promise<{ cancelled: boolean }>;

  /** Interrupt the currently-running turn. Unchanged. */
  interrupt(): Promise<void>;

  /** Terminate session. Unchanged. */
  close(): Promise<void>;
}
```

### Capabilities (descriptive, not opt-in)

```ts
interface ProviderCapabilities {
  // ... existing fields
  /** True if the underlying CLI accepts user messages mid-turn. App may use this to gate "type while working" UI. */
  concurrentSend: boolean;
  /** True if `cancel(uuid)` can remove queued messages on this provider. */
  cancelQueuedMessage: boolean;
}
```

Capability flags describe *what the provider can do*. They do not gate API access — `send()` and `cancel()` are always callable. They are advisory for apps that want to adapt their UI.

### Behavioral contracts

**Claude adapter:**
- `send(msg)` generates UUID with `randomUUID()`, returns `{uuid, result}` immediately. Writes `{type:"user", uuid, message:{role:"user", content:msg}, parent_tool_use_id:null}` to stdin regardless of `_state`. Removes the `_state !== "idle"` guard.
- `result` resolves when the next `result` event arrives. Multiple in-flight sends MAY resolve with the same TurnResult.
- `cancel(uuid)` writes `control_request {subtype:'cancel_async_message', message_uuid: uuid}` and awaits the matching `control_response`. Returns `{ cancelled }` from the CLI's response.

**Codex adapter:**
- `send(msg)` generates UUID locally (not part of Codex protocol but returned to caller for parity), returns `{uuid, result}`. Writes `turn/start` regardless of `_state`. Removes the guard.
- When `send()` is called during an active turn, Codex's `app-server` merges the second `turn/start` into the active turn as a new `userMessage` item — different mechanism from Claude's mid-turn drain but functionally equivalent (the model addresses both messages in one response). Verified end-to-end via the concurrent smoke test against codex-cli 0.130.0.
- `result` resolves on the next `turn/completed` event after the write.
- `cancel(uuid)` returns `{cancelled: false}`. Codex's official protocol bindings (`codex app-server generate-ts`) confirm there's no per-message cancel in the entire `ClientRequest` union — only `turn/interrupt` (kills whole turn), `turn/steer` (inject into active turn), and `thread/rollback` (drop N turns). `capabilities.cancelQueuedMessage: false`.

**Other providers (cursor, gemini, openclaw, opencode, pi):**
- Until audited (Phase 5), keep the existing guard. `send()` throws when called concurrently. `cancel()` returns `{cancelled: false}`.
- Per-provider audit task lifts the guard where the upstream CLI supports it.

**process adapter:**
- No protocol; can't promise anything about concurrent stdin writes. Keep the guard. `concurrentSend: false`.

### TurnResult contract change

Update the JSDoc on `TurnResult` and `send()` to make this explicit:

```
When concurrentSend is true and multiple send() calls occur during a single
turn, the CLI may merge their messages into one turn's processing — in which
case the Promises returned by each send() resolve with the SAME TurnResult
object. Callers cannot assume 1:1 correspondence between send() calls and
TurnResults.
```

### State machine

Today `_state` transitions: `idle → thinking → tool_executing → ... → idle`. With concurrent send, `_state` no longer gates writes. Keep `_state` for observability (UI can show "thinking") but stop using it as a write barrier.

Add to docs: "session.state reflects the most recent observed lifecycle event, not whether send() is callable. With concurrentSend providers, send() is always callable while state is not 'closed'."

## Risks

1. **Protocol corruption if a non-concurrent CLI gets a mid-turn write.** Mitigated by per-provider capability flag and keeping the guard for unverified providers.
2. **TurnResult ambiguity.** Two concurrent `send()` calls may both resolve with the same merged TurnResult. Documented; app needs to track UUIDs locally.
3. **`cancel(uuid)` race.** Between the moment the app decides to cancel and the moment the CLI processes the control_request, the message may already have been dequeued. `{cancelled: false}` is the honest answer — the app should treat it as "too late."
4. **Codex queueing is informal.** We confirmed empirically via transcript that it works, but the JSON-RPC protocol doesn't formally document it. Risk that a Codex CLI update breaks the behavior. Mitigation: integration test that pins behavior, runs on a known-good Codex version.

## Out of scope (future work)

- **Priority sends.** Claude's queue has `now / next / later`. Could expose as `send(msg, {priority})` later; not in v1.
- **`peek` / queue listing.** No protocol surface for Claude; app-side tracking covers most use cases. Revisit if a real need surfaces.
- **In-adapter buffer for non-concurrent providers.** Would require implementing queue, priority, and dispatch logic for each adapter. Defer until an app actually needs it.

# Inference speed: Standard, Fast, and Ultrafast

`ProviderConfig.serviceTier` selects inference speed independently of the model
and reasoning effort. It works with `execute()`, new sessions, and resumed
sessions. Omitting it preserves native defaults; `"default"` explicitly selects
Standard. Agent Ex never enables a paid tier automatically.

| Provider | Tier IDs | Minimum CLI for this integration |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Codex | `default`, `priority` (`fast` alias), `ultrafast`, and future catalog IDs | 0.163.0 |
| Claude Code | `default`, `fast` | 2.1.205 |

Paid-tier availability depends on the model, account, organization settings, and
capacity. Fast and Ultrafast have different usage costs. Check the provider's
current terms: [Codex speed](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/speed),
[OpenAI API Fast](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/fast-mode),
[OpenAI API Ultrafast](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/ultrafast-mode),
and [Claude Code Fast](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/fast-mode).

## Selecting a tier

```ts
import { getProvider } from "@agentex/agent";

const codex = getProvider("codex");
const fast = await codex.execute({
  cwd: "/path/to/project",
  prompt: "Explain the failing test",
  config: { serviceTier: "fast" },
});

// Change an existing thread to Standard, preserving its identity and history.
const standard = await codex.execute({
  cwd: "/path/to/project",
  prompt: "Now fix it",
  sessionParams: fast.sessionParams,
  config: { serviceTier: "default" },
});

// Claude Fast requires an explicit supported Opus model.
const claude = getProvider("claude");
const session = await claude.createSession!({
  cwd: "/path/to/project",
  config: { model: "opus", serviceTier: "fast" },
});
try {
  const turn = await (await session.send("Explain the failing test")).result;
  console.log(turn.serviceTier);
} finally {
  await session.close();
}
```

A session's configured tier applies to all its turns. To change it, close and
resume the session with a new config. `SendOptions` does not offer a tier override:
concurrent messages can join an already running inference turn, whose speed
cannot be changed by steering it.

Other providers do not implement this field. Check
`provider.capabilities.serviceTiers` before offering a speed control.
`probeCapabilities()` checks the installed CLI version; it does not establish
account entitlement.

## Discovering choices

```ts
const models = await codex.listModels!({
  cwd: "/path/to/project",
  config: { extraArgs: ["--profile", "work"] },
  cacheTtlMs: 30_000,
});
for (const model of models) {
  console.log(model.id, model.defaultServiceTier, model.serviceTiers);
}
```

`ProviderModel.serviceTiers` contains `{ id, name, description?, availability?,
reason? }`. `defaultServiceTier` preserves Codex's advertised default. Missing
metadata means unknown, and an empty native tier list permits only Standard.
Codex catalog IDs are retained, with Fast normalized to `priority`.

`availability` is `available`, `unavailable`, or `unknown`. A model advertising
Fast is not proof that this account can use it; paid tiers normally report
`unknown`. Disabled Codex feature flags or a disabled Claude Fast environment
report `unavailable`. Discovery honors the selected binary, effective environment,
endpoint, supplied Claude settings, and Codex config/profile. Cache keys include
those inputs and hash credential values rather than keeping them in the key.
Native credential-file metadata also participates, so an in-place login change
does not reuse the previous account's catalog. OS keychain changes are not
observed by this file fingerprint. Use `cacheTtlMs: 0` to refresh; the native CLI
may still maintain its own catalog cache.

Claude offers Fast for the supported Opus families (5.5, 5, 4.8), including the
`opus` and `opus[1m]` aliases and their endpoint/environment mappings. An implicit model, Sonnet,
Haiku, or an unrecognized model ID fails Fast validation before inference. This
prevents Claude Code from silently upgrading the model when Fast is enabled.
Claude does not offer Ultrafast. Known Bedrock (including Mantle), Vertex/Agent
Platform, Foundry, and Claude Platform on AWS routing marks Fast unavailable and
rejects an explicit Fast request. These checks use the effective environment,
including endpoint overrides and supplied `--settings` environment values.

## Observing what actually happened

`ExecutionResult.serviceTier`, `TurnResult.serviceTier`, and
`AgentSession.serviceTier` expose the same state:

```ts
interface ServiceTierState {
  requested: string | null; // explicit config, e.g. "fast"
  selected: string | null;  // native configuration, e.g. Codex "priority"
  effective: string | null; // observed processing speed, otherwise null
  reason: string | null;    // native fallback notification, when supplied
}
```

Updates arrive as `{ type: "service_tier", update: Partial<ServiceTierState> }`
stream events. Effective speed resets each turn; results retain that turn's
snapshot even when another send starts. Subagent speed reports do not overwrite
the root session's state.

Codex start/resume and settings notifications establish `selected`. They do not
prove processing speed. `effective` remains null unless the runtime forwards an
actual API `response.completed.service_tier` report. Claude's `usage.speed`
reports `fast` or `standard` (normalized to `default`); Fast-mode notifications
surface their explanation without guessing the actual tier. A run may request
Fast and report Standard after a native fallback. No speed observation means
unknown, not Standard. These observations are not a billing receipt.

## Validation, settings, and transport

Explicit invalid or unsupported selections throw `ServiceTierConfigurationError`
before inference. Its `code` is `invalid_tier`, `unsupported_runtime`,
`unsupported_model`, `conflicting_settings`, `unavailable`, or `discovery_failed`.
Provider errors encountered during inference still follow the usual execution
and turn error paths. Unset tiers preserve compatibility with older runtimes.

Codex passes the canonical tier through startup config and explicitly through
`thread/start`, `thread/resume`, and `turn/start`. It checks feature flags and the
actual selected model's catalog before starting a turn. A policy rejection on
resume is never retried as a new conversation. Explicit `default` suppresses a
saved or catalog-selected paid tier.

When `execute()` has an explicit `serviceTier`, it runs one bounded turn through
`app-server`, including timeout/cancellation, output, usage, session identity,
and workspace handling. This is necessary because native `codex exec resume`
restores the saved tier over a startup `-c` override. With no `serviceTier`,
existing execution routing is preserved: app-server for `skillDirs`, otherwise
native `codex exec`. Explicit tiers also preserve process-scoped skill isolation.
For typed-tier executions, raw
`extraArgs` must be valid for `app-server`/root config; exec-only flags do not
apply. Prefer the typed options.

Typed-tier executions preserve the cross-directory resume guard: changing `cwd`
or preparing a worktree starts a fresh thread and reports `clearSession: true`.
Direct `createSession()` resumes explicitly select the requested `cwd`. Both
paths verify the native working directory before inference. Cancellation covers
the startup handshake; each startup RPC also has a 30-second bound independent
of the execution deadline. Native cumulative token notifications are converted
to per-turn input, output, and cached-token usage, excluding resumed history and
child threads. The fallback log scanner honors the child's Codex home.

Claude translates the selection to `fastMode: true/false`. If `extraArgs` already
contains `--settings`, Agent Ex reads the final settings argument (inline JSON or
file, matching CLI precedence) and preserves its other fields. The merged JSON
is staged in a private file with mode `0600` and removed when execution ends or
the session closes/exits. Existing settings contents are not copied into argv.
Global settings files are never rewritten. Native organization policy and
fallback behavior remain in force.

Contradictory explicit raw settings are rejected: Codex `service_tier` must agree
with `config.serviceTier`, and Claude's supplied `fastMode` must agree. Known
Fast-disabling environment and per-session settings also fail validation rather
than being overridden.

Gateway configs accept the same field on both the default `agent` and named
`agents` entries:

```yaml
agent:
  provider: claude
  cwd: /path/to/project
  model: opus
  serviceTier: fast
```
